Preprint. Under review.
Joint Optimization for Greedy Longest-match Tokenization
Adhiraj Singh∗
Deepanshu Mody∗
Ghina Al Shdaifat
Hamza Alshamy
Center for Data Science, New York University
New York, NY, USA
{as19687,dm6262,gha2009,ha2486}@nyu.edu
Adam Wiemerslage
Varshini Reddy
Craig W. Schmidt
Kensho Technologies
Cambridge, MA, USA
{adam.wiemerlsage,varshini.bogolu,craig.schmidt}@kensho.com
Abstract
Recent work shows that subword vocabularies can be trained to directly
optimize compression for a specific inference rule, rather than relying
on a greedy merge heuristic like Byte Pair Encoding (BPE). For example,
ToaST targets split-tree inference and ConvexTok targets shortest-path
inference. We extend this approach to greedy left-to-right (GL2R) longest-
match decoding, the fast and widely used inference rule of WordPiece. We
introduce Joint Optimization for Greedy Longest-match Tokenization
(JOLT), which formulates GL2R vocabulary learning as an integer program
(IP) over vocabulary-selection and segmentation-choice variables. The
key ingredient is a set of greedy-consistency constraints that force each
pretoken’s segmentation to match exactly what GL2R produces under
the selected vocabulary, making the optimized token count equal to the
count realized at deployment. To solve the IP at scale, we use a linear
program (LP) relaxation that escalates only unresolved pretokens to higher-
order segmentations. The relaxation is near-integral: rounded solutions
fall within 0.008–0.176% of the LP lower bound, certifying near-optimal
GL2R compression on the training scope. The same bound reveals that
BPE already sits within 1–2% of the LP lower bound on the training scope,
confirming the heuristic is near-optimal for GL2R inference; JOLT closes
89.6–99.4% of this gap. On held-out validation across four training scopes
(N ∈{100k, 200k, 300k, 400k}) and two vocabulary sizes (|V| ∈{32k, 64k}),
JOLT yields up to 0.78% fewer tokens than BPE, with gains growing with
scope. Together, these results show that most of the compression headroom
between BPE and the LP lower bound can be recovered through inference-
aligned vocabulary optimization.
1
Introduction
Most NLP tasks use a tokenizer as a first step, converting text into a sequence of tokens
drawn from a fixed vocabulary. Byte Pair Encoding (BPE; Sennrich et al., 2016) is among the
most frequently used subword tokenizers; WordPiece (Wu et al., 2016; Schuster & Nakajima,
2012) and UnigramLM (Kudo, 2018) are also widely deployed. Originally proposed as a
general-purpose compression algorithm (Gage, 1994) and later adapted for NLP (Sennrich
et al., 2016), BPE greedily builds a vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent
adjacent token pair until it reaches its target size. Producing shorter token sequences is
valuable for language models: it increases the amount of text in a given context window,
and reduces inference cost. While the effect of compression on downstream accuracy is still
contested (Gallé, 2019; Rust et al., 2021; Ali et al., 2024; Goldman et al., 2024; Schmidt et al.,
2024), its practical benefits alone make compression worth optimizing.
∗These authors contributed equally and are the corresponding authors.
1
arXiv:2607.23362v1  [cs.CL]  25 Jul 2026


--- Page 2 ---
Preprint. Under review.
Recent work shows that vocabulary training need not be limited to greedy merge heuristics:
ToaST (Schmidt et al., 2026) and ConvexTok (Tempus et al., 2026) show that one can directly
optimize compression by formulating vocabulary training as an integer program (IP),
relaxing it to a linear program (LP), and extracting a discrete vocabulary via rounding.1 This
re-frames tokenizer design from heuristic, procedure-driven training to an inference-specific
optimization problem. There is therefore no single notion of “best compressing tokenizer”
independent of inference rule; optimality must be stated relative to the inference rule.
Greedy left-to-right (GL2R) longest-match decoding is a simple and fast tokenization in-
ference rule, most commonly used by WordPiece. Given a vocabulary, GL2R scans the
input left to right and at each position emits the longest vocabulary token matching the
bytes starting there, advancing by its length; with a full set of single-byte tokens in the
vocabulary, this always succeeds without unknown tokens. Uzan et al. (2024) show that
GL2R is effective even when applied to vocabularies trained by other methods. However,
there has not been a vocabulary construction technique designed specifically to work with
GL2R. We develop Joint Optimization for Greedy Longest-match Tokenization (JOLT),
which follows the same high-level recipe as ToaST and ConvexTok (integer program →
LP relaxation →rounding to a fixed vocabulary) but formulates the model specifically for
GL2R inference, making the optimized token count equal to the one realized at deployment.
Empirically, JOLT reduces greedy-L2R token counts on held-out text by up to 0.78% relative
to BPE at equal vocabulary size across four training scopes (N ∈{100k, 200k, 300k, 400k}),
with larger scopes consistently yielding equal or better compression. Beyond the compres-
sion gains, the LP bound provides a structural diagnostic: BPE’s token count on the training
scope falls within 1–2% of the LP lower bound, revealing that the BPE heuristic is already
near-optimal under GL2R inference. JOLT closes 89.6–99.4% of this gap, and its rounded
vocabularies fall within 0.008–0.176% of the LP bound, so rounding loses almost none of the
LP-achievable compression. JOLT’s small margin over BPE on the held-out validation set
therefore reflects the limited headroom above the LP bound, not a rounding artifact.
2
JOLT Model
JOLT formulates vocabulary learning as a joint integer program over two coupled choices:
which candidate tokens enter the vocabulary, and which candidate segmentation of each
pretoken is selected. Under GL2R, the longest matching vocabulary token wins at each posi-
tion, so a segmentation is GL2R-realizable only for vocabularies in which no longer token
intrudes at any segment boundary. Enforcing this validity condition explicitly (Section 2.4)
is what couples the vocabulary-selection and segmentation-choice variables. Because the
number of candidate segmentations grows exponentially in pretoken length, JOLT does
not instantiate them all up front, but initially works with a small number of candidate
segmentations per pretoken, adding more as needed.
2.1
Pretokens, segmentations, and costs
Pretokens.
We first segment the training corpus into pretokens using a regular expression2
and aggregate identical pretokens by count. Let P be the set of aggregated pretokens in the
training data, with frequency cp ∈N for each pretoken p ∈P. We work with byte-level
tokenization, so we define np = |p| as the byte length of pretoken p.
For vocabulary training we retain the N highest-count pretokens; throughout the IP below,
P denotes this restricted top-N set with counts cp, not the full pretoken vocabulary.
Segmentations.
A segmentation s partitions a pretoken p into contiguous, non-empty
candidate tokens. We depict example segmentations visually divided by |, e.g. segmentation

ton et al., 2025; Kastreva et al., 2026), so corpus-scale work solves an LP relaxation and rounds to a
fixed vocabulary rather than optimizing the full IP.
2We use a length limited version of the GPT-4o regex. See Appendix C for more details.

s = ta | ble for pretoken p = table. The order of s is the number of pieces (tokens) in the
partition. An order-r segmentation is determined by choosing r −1 internal split positions
among the np −1 byte gaps, so there are exactly (np−1
r−1 ) order-r candidates for p. Summing
over orders shows the total grows exponentially in np:

(1)
In practice, however, a compression-oriented vocabulary will tokenize most pretokens
with a low-order segmentation, so only a small fraction of the 2np−1 candidates need to be
explicitly instantiated.
To avoid the exponential number of potential segmentations, we instantiate only segmen-
tations up to a bounded order per pretoken. Let κp denote the maximum segmentation
order currently instantiated for p. For a given κp, let Sp be the finite set of segmentation
choices for p: all s with order(s) ≤κp, together with a fallback F. The fallback is not itself a
segmentation of p; choosing F means that none of the currently instantiated segmentations
suffice and the solver would prefer a partition of order greater than κp. We initially set
κp = 2, so Sp contains only the whole pretoken, all order-2 segmentations, and F; these are
the only segmentation options for p in the first round. When the solver selects F for p, κp is
incremented and the next order of segmentations is appended to Sp (Section 2.5). Thus,
|Sp| =
κp
∑
r=1
np −1
r −1

+ 1.
(2)
Escalation then increases κp and enriches Sp only for those pretokens (Section 2.5), rather
than instantiating higher-order segmentations for every p ∈P up front. This selective
escalation avoids instantiating high-order segmentations unnecessarily, reducing LP size
and solve time.
Tokens and costs.
Training proceeds in a sequence of rounds. In each round, every pretoken
p has a fixed limit κp on segmentation order, with a fixed finite set Sp. We build and solve
the IP (or its LP relaxation); pretokens that select the fallback F trigger an increase in κp and
a rebuild before the next round (Section 2.5).
Figure 1(a) gives an example for the pretoken p = table with np = 5. There are 2np−1 = 16
potential segmentations, but with the initial κp = 2 only six are instantiated choices: the
whole pretoken, four order-2 segmentations, and F. When a pretoken selects the fallback, its
κp is increased by one in the next round and those new candidates are appended (Section 2.5).
Figure 1(b) shows the six extra order-3 segmentations added when κp increases to 3; all
2np−1 segmentations enter Sp only if κp reaches np.
Let B denote the set of all 256 single-byte tokens which are always retained in the extracted
vocabulary (Equation (8)) to avoid unknown tokens. For each p ∈P and non-fallback s ∈Sp,

In intermediate rounds, cost(p, F) = κp + 1 is intentionally one token above the largest cost
among currently instantiated segmentations of order ≤κp, so any non-fallback segmentation
is strictly cheaper than F. Section 2.5 uses this pricing to decide when to enrich Sp; the final
round sets cost(p, F) = np so the reported score reflects the worst-case GL2R token count
for any remaining fallback pretokens once Sp has converged.
2.2
Decision variables and objective
Vocabulary-selection variables.
For each candidate token t ∈T, define
xt ∈{0, 1}
∀t ∈T,
(5)
where xt = 1 means token t is in the vocabulary. For example, for pretoken table, xtab = 1
means tab is globally available as a candidate token.
Segmentation-choice variables.
For each p ∈P and each s ∈Sp, we introduce a binary
decision variable
zp,s ∈{0, 1}
∀p ∈P, ∀s ∈Sp,
(6)
where zp,s = 1 indicates that segmentation s is selected for pretoken p; the greedy-
consistency constraints (Section 2.4) then enforce that the active segmentation is exactly
the one GL2R produces. Because cost(p, s) < cost(p, F) for every non-fallback s, selecting
F (i.e., zp,F = 1 in the integer problem, or LP mass on zp,F ≥θ in the relaxation; we use
θ = 0.01) is the signal that the current Sp is too coarse; Section 2.5 acts on that signal to
increase κp and reduce the use of fallbacks.
Optimization objective.
We minimize the corpus-weighted token count: each pretoken p
selects exactly one segmentation s ∈Sp, paying cost(p, s) tokens, weighted by the aggre-
gated count cp. The objective is:

Linking constraint.
For non-fallback s, recall from Section 2.1 that Ep,s is the set of tokens
t used in segmentation s of pretoken p. A segmentation can be activated only if all of its
tokens are selected in the vocabulary:
zp,s ≤xt
∀p ∈P, ∀s ∈Sp \ {F}, ∀t ∈Ep,s.
(11)
For example, splitting table as ta | ble requires both ta and ble to be in the vocabulary.
The blue rows of Figure 2 show this for two example segmentations.
2.4
Greedy-consistency constraints
The feasibility constraints above (Equations (8) to (11)) ensure budget compliance and
that an activated segmentation uses tokens selected in the vocabulary, but they do not yet
enforce that it is the segmentation GL2R would actually produce for the given vocabulary.
A segmentation s is GL2R-realizable (under vocabulary V) if it is exactly the segmentation
GL2R longest-prefix decoding emits on pretoken p. Greedy-consistency means that every
choice with zp,s = 1 is GL2R-realizable; we enforce this with Equation (13).
A segment g is one contiguous piece of a segmentation s; for s = ta | b | le the segments are
ta, b, and le. Let G−
s denote the non-final segments of s (here ta and b); the final segment has
nothing downstream to displace, so it imposes no constraint. For byte strings u, v we write
u ⪯v if u is a prefix of v, and u ≺v if additionally u̸ = v. Under GL2R, s is GL2R-realizable
only if at the start of each non-final segment, no longer vocabulary token extends past that
segment, otherwise GL2R would emit the longer token and shift all downstream boundaries.
The red rows of Figure 2 illustrate this for two example segmentations.
Consider a non-final segment g ∈G−
s , and let w be the suffix of p that starts at g (so w
begins with g, i.e. g ⪯w). For example, with p = table and g = ta we have w = table;
with g = b we have w = ble. The forbidden-prefix set Lp,s,g comprises candidate tokens that
strictly extend g while still matching the upcoming bytes of p:
Lp,s,g =

t ∈T : g ≺t ⪯w
	
∀p ∈P, ∀s ∈Sp \ {F}, ∀g ∈G−
s .
(12)
For p = table, g = ta, and w = table, Equation (12) yields Lp,s,g = {tab, tabl, table}.
Note g ≺t alone is not enough: tax extends ta but is not in Lp,s,g, since tax̸ ⪯table means
GL2R never considers it here. A forbidden longer prefix need not be a segment of s (e.g.
tab ∈Lp,s,g for ta | ble although tab is not one of its segments).
If any t ∈Lp,s,g is in the vocabulary, s cannot be selected:
zp,s ≤1 −xt
∀p ∈P, ∀s ∈Sp \ {F}, ∀g ∈G−
s , ∀t ∈Lp,s,g.
(13)
Together with the linking constraint Equation (11), which guarantees each segment string is
itself in the vocabulary, Equation (13) ensures that whenever zp,s = 1 each chosen segment
is the longest vocabulary match at its start position, exactly the segmentation GL2R longest-
prefix decoding emits with vocabulary V.

2.5
Fallback-driven escalation
Equation (13) must be enforced for every segmentation variable we instantiate, so the size
of the IP in Equations (7) to (13) is driven by |Sp| in each round. Section 2.1 explained why
naively instantiating all orders for every pretoken in the top-N set would introduce too
many variables and constraints, making the LP slow to solve; here we describe the schedule
that keeps each solve tractable while preserving a globally coupled objective.
Fallback as model-size control.
Every pretoken has a distinct F ∈Sp with variable
zp,F; setting it to 1 pays the higher cost(p, F) rather than committing to any instantiated
segmentation. This is not a soft penalty but a model-size control: it lets us omit higher-order
segmentations until the solver signals the current family is too coarse for p.
Fallback-driven iterative escalation.
Training solves a sequence of LP relaxations of
the globally coupled IP, each with the same structure Equations (8) to (13) and objective
Equation (7), but with pretoken segmentation sets Sp growing from round to round, and the
candidate set T recomputed accordingly.
Round 1. For every p ∈P, set κp = 2 and initialize Sp to the unsplit pretoken, all order-2
segmentations (one internal split per byte gap), and F. To shrink the first LP, the Ntop=8000
highest-count pretokens start with κp=1 (whole pretoken and F only): these extremely
frequent tokens (common words like the, is, in, and common punctuation) carry the bulk of
corpus mass and are near-certain vocabulary members as whole units regardless of budget,
making their order-2 splits almost never worthwhile; omitting them removes a large fraction
of variables and greedy-consistency rows (Equation (13)) with little empirical impact. Any
pretoken that nonetheless activates F is promoted to the full order-2 family before the next
round.
Escalation loop. After the solution of each LP (Section 2.6) with optimal fractional values
(x⋆, z⋆) in round i, read off the fallback-active set Fi = {p ∈P : z⋆
p,F ≥θ} from the fractional
solution. Only pretokens in Fi have κp incremented (up to cap M=3), their order-(κp+1)
segmentations appended to Sp, T and the full IP rebuilt, and re-solved; Figure 1(b) illustrates
the order-3 segmentations added for p = table ∈Fi. The loop continues until Fi = ∅or no
κp changes.
Final repricing. When the structure stabilizes, one last solve freezes each Sp and sets
cost(p, F) = np via Equation (4), so resolved pretokens carry their exact GL2R inference
cost while any remaining fallback mass is assigned a conservative byte-level upper bound.
LP relaxation and vocabulary extraction from the final fractional solution are described in
the next subsection.
2.6
LP relaxation and weighted rounding
The IP instances in Equations (7) to (13) are too large to solve to optimality at corpus scale,
even after iterative enrichment of the segmentation families. Following ToaST, JOLT works
with an LP relaxation that replaces the binary domains in Equations (5) to (6) by
0 ≤xt ≤1
∀t ∈T,
(14)
0 ≤zp,s ≤1
∀p ∈P, ∀s ∈Sp.
(15)
Solving the resulting LP with Gurobi (Gurobi Optimization, LLC, 2026) yields optimal
fractional values (x⋆, z⋆). Relaxing integrality allows segmentation mass to split fractionally
across Sp, but the relaxation remains globally coupled across pretokens: high-count p still
pulls token mass toward compressing segmentations that survive GL2R linking and greedy-
consistency coupling. In practice the final-round solution is empirically near-integral on our
instances (many x⋆
t near 0 or 1), which makes a simple rounding rule effective to construct
a budget-feasible vocabulary under Equation (9) without solving the full IP to optimality.
The optimal objective value is a valid lower bound on the corresponding instantiated IP
objective.
6


--- Page 7 ---
Preprint. Under review.
Contribution-based rounding.
We extract the vocabulary from (x⋆, z⋆) using the
contribution-based weighted rounding of ToaST. The rule is unchanged: although JOLT’s
segmentation variables zp,s range over GL2R-realizable segmentations rather than split-
tree ones, rounding treats them only as generic segmentation variables, so the procedure
transfers verbatim. Tokens with x⋆
t ≥1 −ϵ are admitted to V outright (Appendix B); the
remaining budget is filled from the fractional tier by objective contribution C⋆
t , the count-
weighted z⋆-mass flowing through t (Equation (16) in Appendix B). Selection therefore
favors tokens the relaxation already used to compress high-frequency pretokens, rather
than tokens with large x⋆
t but little segmentation support. Inference applies GL2R decoding
with V.
3
Experimental Setup
3.1
Data and pretokenization
We train and evaluate all tokenizers on MiniPile (Kaddour, 2023), a subset of The Pile (Gao
et al., 2020), using a document-level 75%/25% train/validation split. Both splits are pre-
tokenized with GPT4O_REGEX_16 (details in Appendix C), which segments text into words,
numbers, punctuation, and whitespace runs; tokens cannot cross pretoken boundaries. We
write Pval for the full set of aggregated pretoken types on the validation holdout (100% of
validation count mass); all token counts, % decrease, and Rényi efficiency in Section 4 are
evaluated on Pval.
3.2
Baselines and Configurations
Baselines.
BPE, WordPiece, and UnigramLM are trained on the full training corpus using
standard HuggingFace pipelines. BPE-native decodes with the standard BPE merge rule;
BPE-greedy applies GL2R longest-prefix decoding to the same vocabulary, isolating the effect
of inference rule from vocabulary construction. WordPiece-greedy and UnigramLM-greedy
analogously pair standard vocabularies with GL2R decoding at evaluation. UnigramLM-
greedy serves as a diagnostic for training-objective mismatch: it applies the same GL2R
inference as JOLT but was trained to maximize unigram language-model likelihood rather
than minimize token count, so its substantially higher token counts reflect training-objective
divergence. All methods are evaluated at matched vocabulary sizes |V| ∈{32,000, 64,000};
% improvements are relative to BPE-native merge decoding.
JOLT
configurations.
We
evaluate
JOLT
at
four
training
scopes
(N
∈
{100k, 200k, 300k, 400k}) and both vocabulary budgets, with all runs capped at es-
calation order M=3.3 Because corpus-scale LP solves are far more expensive than standard
baseline training, JOLT trains exclusively on the top-N pretokens (the set P of Section 2.1),
while baselines train on the full distribution; both are evaluated on the same Pval. Pretoken
frequencies are highly skewed, so even the smallest scope (N=100k) covers ≈95.8% of
training count mass, rising to ≈98.3% at N=400k; nevertheless, this asymmetry can
disadvantage JOLT for tail pretokens not seen during optimization, so reported validation
margins may understate its compression quality on the training scope where LP certificates
apply. The two larger scopes (N=300k and N=400k) use the round-2-only protocol of
Section 3.3 to assess training scope sensitivity.
3.3
Extended-scope protocol (N=300k and N=400k)
Full-pipeline runs at N=100k/200k provide our LP optimality certificates; extended scopes
at N=300k/400k use a round-2-only protocol within our compute budget and are reported
to assess whether validation compression continues to improve as N grows, not to claim
an equivalent final-round bound. At N=300k and N=400k the final repricing LP becomes
prohibitively expensive within our compute budget (See the full breakdown of solve times

at M=3 (≈0.05% apart). Higher order adds substantial LP size with no compression gain.

Table 4, we report the raw Gurobi iter-2 LP objective and the greedy-L2R token count
on P from the iter-2 vocabulary. We do not correct the iter-2 fallback cost (κp+1=3) to the
final-round byte-level penalty np: doing so after the fact would invalidate the relaxation
bound, since z⋆was optimized under the original costs (Appendix I).
Because the full pipeline remains affordable at N=100k and N=200k, we use those runs as
a sanity check: extracting the iter-2 vocabulary and rounded count from saved checkpoints
recovers full-pipeline rounded objectives to within 0.03% and validation token counts to
within ≈0.5M tokens (Appendix I), justifying the round-2-only protocol at larger N.
4
Results and Analysis
4.1
Optimality Bounds and Gap Closure
Figure 3 shows the LP bound, rounded JOLT token count, and BPE-greedy on the training
scope P (not on Pval) for the four full-pipeline runs (N ∈{100k, 200k}, both vocabulary
budgets). The LP objective is a valid lower bound on achievable GL2R token count under our
formulation, and all four instances solve to OPTIMAL (Appendices D and J). The rounded
score exceeds this LP bound by only 0.008–0.176%, so the extracted vocabularies nearly
attain the relaxation optimum on P. Because rounded JOLT vocabularies sit this close to
the LP bound, any margin over BPE-native on Pval reflects genuine LP-level compression
gains, not rounding loss. On the matched training scope P (not on Pval, where tail pretokens
outside P dilute the comparison), JOLT closes 89.6–99.4% of the BPE-greedy-to-LP gap,
confirming most achievable compression under our formulation is recovered. BPE-greedy
already sits near the LP lower bound on P, which is why heuristic training leaves only a
small absolute margin on Pval. Intuitively, BPE’s left-to-right merge order naturally favors
longer, more frequent substrings, which aligns structurally with GL2R’s longest-match rule.
Even though BPE was not designed for GL2R, the two procedures share a preference for
greedy length maximization that keeps BPE close to the GL2R-optimal bound.

4.2
Validation Compression Across Training Scopes
Table 1 reports greedy-L2R intrinsic metrics on Pval for all four training scopes. Rows
marked † use the round-2-only protocol (Section 3.3) and report validation compression
only; LP optimality certificates come from the full pipeline at N=100k/200k (Section 4.1).
At |V|=32k, JOLT beats BPE-native at every evaluated scope: +0.59% at N=100k, +0.77%
at N=200k, +0.76% at N=300k, and +0.78% at N=400k. At |V|=64k, whether JOLT beats
BPE-native depends entirely on scope: N=100k trails by 0.63%, while N ≥200k consistently
beats it with the margin growing from +0.23% to +0.31% as N increases. BPE-native
and BPE-greedy differ by only 0.08% at both vocabulary budgets, confirming that for
BPE vocabularies the inference rule is almost irrelevant to compression. The gap between
BPE and JOLT therefore reflects vocabulary construction, not inference-rule mismatch.
WordPiece-greedy, despite being designed for GL2R inference, attains worse compression
than BPE-native (−0.42% at 32k, −0.25% at 64k), consistent with its training objective—
maximizing unigram language-model likelihood rather than minimizing token count—
diverging from compression minimization. The rate of improvement with N differs by
vocabulary budget: at |V|=32k gains plateau near N=200k but show a slight further increase
at N=400k (+0.78%), while at |V|=64k compression improves more steadily through
N=400k (+0.31%). The smaller budget saturates earlier because 32k tokens already cover a
large fraction of the high-frequency pretoken tail at N=200k, whereas the larger vocabulary
has more slots to account for the tail of lower frequency pretokens. Fallback mass after
round 1 stays below 1.6% of training count, halves after order-3 escalation, and validation
counts improve monotonically with each round; full diagnostics are in Appendix F. In
Appendices G and H we compare rank-frequency profiles and token-length distributions
across tokenizers; the overall profiles are largely similar, with the main structural signature
being a modest shift toward length-1 tokens under JOLT.
5
Conclusion
We developed a vocabulary construction method tailored to GL2R longest-match decoding,
a widely deployed inference rule that lacked an inference-specific training method. JOLT
fills this gap with a joint integer program whose greedy-consistency constraints force each
pretoken’s segmentation to match exactly what GL2R realizes under the chosen vocabulary.
The optimizer behaves as designed: rounded JOLT vocabularies close 89.6–99.4% of the
BPE-greedy-to-LP gap on full-pipeline runs. Yet the headroom is small: BPE already sits
within 1–2% of the bound, because its left-to-right merge order rewards the long, frequent
9


--- Page 10 ---
Preprint. Under review.
substrings that GL2R also prefers at decode time. The residual gap is driven primarily by
vocabulary construction rather than the inference rule. Thus, JOLT’s margin — up to 0.78%
fewer held-out tokens, increasing with scope — comes from reshaping the vocabulary, not
from changing inference.
The lasting contribution is therefore not the size of the margin but the ability to certify
it relative to an LP lower bound. The LP bound separates optimizer quality from the
headroom the inference rule allows, turning “how much better can a GL2R tokenizer be?”
from an open question into a measured one. It also provides a reusable test for whether an
inference-specific optimizer is worth building for any other decoding rule.
Limitations
All experiments use MiniPile, a predominantly English corpus, with a single train/vali-
dation split and a fixed regex pretokenizer. Optimality claims are relative to the pretoken
boundaries induced by this pretokenizer, and we do not evaluate transfer to languages
without whitespace-delimited words. The IP covers only the top-N pretokens (≈95.8–98.3%
of count-weighted training mass); the tail is excluded entirely from optimization. Within the
training scope, segmentations above order cap M=3 (Section 3.2) are priced conservatively
with np rather than optimized. Our certificates are empirical LP-gap measurements on the
training scope, not proven general approximation bounds: the IP is never solved to integral
optimality, and the rounding step carries no worst-case guarantee. Finally, our evaluation
is intrinsic only. Our contribution lies in the joint modeling of vocabulary construction
and GL2R segmentation, alongside the certification methodology, rather than a claim of
downstream performance.

Contribution-Based Weighted Rounding
We give the full rounding procedure summarized in Section 2.6; it is ToaST’s rule applied to
JOLT’s LP solution (x⋆, z⋆). Let V ⊆T denote the vocabulary with desired size |V|. Partition
T by the LP value x⋆
t :
T1 = {t ∈T : x⋆
t ≥1 −ϵ},
TF = {t ∈T : ϵ < x⋆
t < 1 −ϵ},
T0 = {t ∈T : x⋆
t ≤ϵ},

Preprint. Under review.
with ϵ = 10−6. Every t ∈T1 is admitted into V outright. The budget still requires
β = |V| −|T1| additional tokens, all drawn from the fractional tier TF (tokens in T0 are
discarded).
For each fractional t ∈TF, define the objective contribution
C⋆

p∈P
∑
s∈Sp\{F} : t∈Ep,s
cp z⋆
p,s.
(16)

relaxed objective is already “buying” t via the segmentations that depend on it. Rank TF in
descending order of C⋆
t and take the top β tokens:
V = T1 ∪top-β (TF, C⋆
· ).
By construction, exactly |V| tokens are selected.
C
GPT4O_REGEX_16 Pretokenization Pattern
We use GPT4O_REGEX_16 as the fixed regex pretokenizer for all experiments. This pattern is
based on the publicly available GPT-4o/o200k_base-style tiktoken regex pretokenizer, but
with explicit length caps added for computational tractability. The regex is used only to
create the initial pretoken/count universe; the learned vocabulary is subsequently optimized
by the LP/MIP formulation described in the main text.
The pattern consists of seven alternatives: lower-case-dominant Unicode word spans with
optional contractions, upper-case-dominant Unicode word spans with optional contractions,
numeric chunks of length 1–3, punctuation/symbol runs, newline-associated whitespace,
trailing whitespace, and general whitespace. The bounded version caps word-like spans
through 32-character letter/mark groups and caps punctuation or whitespace runs at 16
characters.
GPT4O_REGEX_PARTS_16 = [
r"[^\r\n\p{L}\p{N}]?"
r"[\p{Lu}\p{Lt}\p{Lm}\p{Lo}\p{M}]{0,32}"
r"[\p{Ll}\p{Lm}\p{Lo}\p{M}]{1,32}"
r"(?i:'s|'t|'re|'ve|'m|'ll|'d)?",
r"[^\r\n\p{L}\p{N}]?"
r"[\p{Lu}\p{Lt}\p{Lm}\p{Lo}\p{M}]{1,32}"
r"[\p{Ll}\p{Lm}\p{Lo}\p{M}]{0,32}"
r"(?i:'s|'t|'re|'ve|'m|'ll|'d)?",
r"\p{N}{1,3}",
r" ?[^\s\p{L}\p{N}]{1,16}[\r\n/]{0,16}",
r"\s{0,15}[\r\n]{1,16}",
r"\s{1,16}(?!\S)",
r"\s{1,16}",
]
GPT4O_REGEX_16 = "|".join(GPT4O_REGEX_PARTS_16)
Listing 1: Bounded GPT-4o-style regex pretokenizer used in our experiments.
In this work, GPT4O_REGEX_16 should therefore be interpreted as a deterministic preprocess-
ing rule, not as a tokenizer training objective or learned vocabulary. Its role is to define
stable pretoken boundaries before candidate segmentation generation, fallback escalation,
and greedy-L2R vocabulary optimization.
D
Gurobi Solver Setup and Reproducibility
All LP relaxations and MIP solves are run on a single host with Gurobi 11.0 (Gurobi
Optimization, LLC, 2026) (academic license), Python 3.11, and the official gurobipy Python
13


--- Page 14 ---
Preprint. Under review.
bindings. We give the exact solver configuration we used so that the experiments can be
reproduced from the pretoken/count universe alone.
Hardware.
Runs are executed on single shared-memory nodes (one solve per node) with
at least 220 GB of RAM. We do not cap Gurobi’s thread count, so it uses all available cores,
between 18 and 30 threads across our runs; we do not pin threads or NUMA nodes. No
GPU is used. The barrier factorization dominates memory: it peaks at roughly 10 GB for the
largest N=100k LP (32k, iter-2/final) and roughly 30 GB for the largest N=200k LP (32k,
iter-2/final), comfortably within the 220–230 GB memory limit we impose.
Solver parameters.
We solve the LP relaxation with Gurobi’s default LP method (con-
current, which on our models selects barrier followed by crossover) and default presolve
and cut settings; we do not override Method, Crossover, Presolve, or Cuts. We set MIPGap=0
and ConcurrentMIP=1. For the final repricing round we rebuild the model with the up-
dated fallback cost (cost(p, F)=np), accept LP warm-start hints from the previous round
(LPWarmStart=2), and raise NumericFocus=2 for tighter numerics; the reported solve times in
Table 2 therefore include this warm start.
Limits.
We impose a per-solve soft memory limit (MemLimit) of 220–230 GB and a generous
wall-clock limit (up to 4 × 105 s for the largest N=200k configuration). Neither limit is bind-
ing: every solve in Table 2 reaches OPTIMAL via barrier, with factorization memory peaking
near 30 GB. Solve time, however, spans three orders of magnitude across configurations,
from 420 s (N=100k, 32k, iter-1) to 337,686.7 s (≈93.8 h; N=200k, 32k, final repricing round),
so the N=200k runs require multi-day budgets while the N=100k runs finish within hours
(largest 32k final, 35,020.9 s). We log Gurobi’s final status, objective bound, simplex/barrier
iteration counts, and final residuals after every solve.
Determinism.
We do not set a solver seed and leave Gurobi’s concurrent LP at its default,
so the LP objective is reproducible only up to floating-point summation order and solver
concurrency (these depend on host and thread count). Given the LP solution, however, the
rest of the pipeline is fully deterministic: contribution-based rounding breaks ties in C⋆
t
lexicographically on t, so the extracted vocabulary is uniquely determined by the (fixed)
pretoken/count input and segmentation-family construction order.
E
Compute Time
Detailed computational results are given in Table 2. The N=200k full-pipeline configuration
(full 2 →3 escalation and a final repricing round) is the most expensive among the full-
pipeline runs: end-to-end about 113 hours of wall-clock time at the 32k vocabulary budget
and about 26 hours at 64k, with the 32k final-round LP alone taking 337,686.7 s (≈93.8 h).
The wall-clock cost is dominated by the final-round LP solve in Table 2; the earlier rounds
and the entire model-build phase together contribute roughly one to two additional hours.
The cheaper N=100k variant runs in approximately 11 hours at 32k and under 3 hours at 64k
(32k final-round LP solve of 35,020.9 s), a ∼10× speedup for only a ∼2.9× smaller constraint
matrix. Within each scope, cost also varies with how binding the budget is: |V|=64k is
cheaper than |V|=32k because the LP is less fractional.

and validation holdout Pval after contribution-based rounding at that stage. We report
both fallback count and weighted mass by stage because they can move differently under
repricing and rounding.

G
Token Rank-Frequency on the Validation Holdout
To test whether JOLT’s compression gains reshape the global vocabulary usage profile or
arise from local segmentation choices, we plot log-log token rank–frequency curves after
greedy-L2R decoding on the full validation holdout Pval (Section 3.1). Each curve ranks
every token emitted on Pval by its count; BPE-greedy uses a vocabulary trained on the full
training holdout, and JOLT curves use the rounded vocabularies from our N=100k and
200k optimization scopes.
At |V|=32k (left panel of Figure 5), all three series overlap across ranks. At |V|=64k (right
panel), the high-frequency head remains aligned but the tails separate: N=200k tracks BPE-
greedy more closely in the rare-token regime than the cheaper N=100k scope, consistent
with its stronger validation margin in Table 1. No series introduces a qualitatively different
Zipf shape; the effect is a modest tail adjustment rather than a wholesale redistribution.

H
Token-Length Distribution: BPE-greedy vs. JOLT
Beyond aggregate token-count metrics, we compare the token-length distribution each vo-
cabulary induces under greedy-L2R decoding on Pval (Section 4.2), because local shifts
in emitted token lengths can accompany even small changes in total count. Figure 6 re-
ports count-weighted shares of output tokens by byte length, for both vocabulary budgets
and the two full-pipeline scopes (N=100k and N=200k). BPE-greedy uses a vocabulary
trained on the full training holdout; relative to it, JOLT shifts a modest amount of count-
weighted mass toward length-1 tokens (by ≈0.9 percentage points at |V|=32k and ≈1.2 at
|V|=64k for the top-100K scope), while every other length stays within about 1 percentage
point. This counter-intuitive increase in single-byte token usage is a consequence of the
greedy-consistency constraints: GL2R can emit a long token at position i only if no longer
vocabulary token starts at i, so JOLT sometimes retains short (including single-byte) tokens
precisely to suppress competing prefixes and allow a longer match a few bytes later, a trade
that reduces total token count even though it raises the single-byte share. Enlarging JOLT’s

range, consistent with the LP using its larger budget on a longer pretoken tail. The shift is
modest relative to BPE-greedy, complementing the token-count margins in Table 1.
I
Extended-Scope Protocol
Round-2-only reporting in Table 4.
For N=300k and N=400k we report the raw Gurobi
iter-2 LP relaxation objective (fallback cost 3) and the true greedy-L2R token count on P from
the iter-2 vocabulary. The LP objective is reported as-is: substituting the true byte-level cost
np for fallback cost 3 in the saved solution z⋆would break the relaxation lower bound—z⋆
was optimized under cost 3—and can inflate gap-closed above 100%.
What the skipped final repricing round would change.
In iter-2 the fallback cost is
cost(p, F) = κp+1=3 for every remaining fallback pretoken, regardless of byte length
np (Equation (4)).
The full pipeline’s final repricing round rebuilds the model with
cost(p, F) = np, re-solves, and may add whole-word tokens for long rare pretokens. To see
why this matters for validation, consider ˙Glipopolysaccharide (np=19 bytes): in iter-2 it
is charged only 3 tokens if it falls back, far below its true cost of 19 bytes, so Gurobi has
no incentive to cover it. The full pipeline corrects this in the final repricing LP, adding
˙Glipopolysaccharide, ˙Gcerebrovascular, and similar rare but long pretokens as whole to-
kens, improving validation scores by approximately 0.46M tokens at |V|=32k/N=100k; the
round-2-only protocol trades this refinement for the ability to optimize over a much larger
pretoken scope.
Sanity check.
Because the full pipeline remains affordable at N=100k and N=200k but
not at N=300k/400k, we validate the round-2-only protocol on the smaller scopes before
trusting it at scale. We extract the iter-2 vocabulary and rounded greedy-L2R count on P
from saved checkpoints for the N=100k and N=200k runs and compare against their full-
pipeline values. Iter-2 rounded objectives agree with full-pipeline rounded objectives to
within 0.03% across all four full-run configurations; validation token counts differ by at most
≈0.5M tokens. This close agreement gives us confidence that the round-2-only numbers at
N=300k and N=400k are comparable to the full-pipeline results.

LP Bound and Rounding Diagnostics (All Training Scopes)
Table 4 reports the LP relaxation objective and the greedy-L2R token count from contribution-
based rounding on the JOLT optimization scope P for all configurations. For the full-pipeline
runs (N ∈{100k, 200k}) the LP objective is the final-round bound with conservative byte-
level fallback cost, and is a valid lower bound on achievable GL2R token count under our
formulation. For the round-2-only runs (N ∈{300k, 400k}) the LP column is the raw Gurobi
iter-2 relaxation objective (fallback cost 3); the rounded column is the true greedy-L2R
count on P with the iter-2 vocabulary (appendix I). These rows close 75.2–86.5% of the
BPE-greedy-to-iter-2-LP slack—informative, but not equivalent to the final-round certificate
above.
